query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying targeted high-temperature thermomechanical processing (hot rolling followed by controlled annealing) to a single-phase Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy will refine its grains and stabilize nano-scale precipitates, leading to enhanced elevated-temperature strength and improved resistance to deformation under extreme environments compared to the as-cast material.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase solid-solution Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy as produced by conventional melting/casting methods.
generation.intervention: High-temperature thermomechanical processing involving hot rolling (to introduce deformation and refine grain boundaries) followed by a controlled annealing treatment (to relieve stresses, refine microstructure further, and stabilize nano-scale precipitates).
generation.conditions: Tested at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) and under extreme-environment stress regimes such as high-temperature tensile and creep tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural grain refinement and the stabilization of nano-scale precipitates.
generation.mechanism: The hot rolling induces dynamic recrystallization that refines grain size and increases grain boundary density, which impedes dislocation motion (grain boundary strengthening). The subsequent controlled annealing encourages the formation and stability of beneficial nano-scale precipitates, contributing to precipitation strengthening, thereby enhancing the alloy’s mechanical performance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast state, the thermomechanically processed alloy will exhibit increased yield and ultimate tensile strength as well as improved creep resistance under elevated temperature and extreme-environment conditions.
generation.baseline: The same Ti–Ni HEA in the as-cast, unprocessed state.
generation.boundary: Applicable to Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloys dominated by titanium and nickel (without significant secondary elemental additions), when subjected to high-temperature mechanical tests (approximately 600–800°C) simulating extreme service conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength improvements and the balance between grain refinement and precipitate stability are uncertain and must be quantified experimentally, as processing parameters may significantly affect the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Ti–Ni HEA samples. Process one set with the proposed high-temperature thermomechanical treatment (hot rolling followed by controlled annealing) while leaving the other set in the as-cast condition. Subject both sets to identical elevated-temperature mechanical tests, such as tensile and creep tests at 600–800°C.
measurements: Grain size analysis via optical/electron microscopy
Nano-scale precipitate characterization using TEM or SEM
Mechanical property measurements including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and creep rate at elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in elevated-temperature strength (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength) and creep resistance compared to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

A series of lightweight Ti-rich MEAs with minor additions of Zr were successfully fabricated through various TMT processing routes. On the basis of the experiment results, the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the alloys are summarized as follows: The XRD results confirm that the structure of the Ti-rich MEAs maintained a single BCC phase not only when they were in an as-cast state but also after they underwent TMT processing. The addition of Zr tended to increase the grain size of cast ingots and compensate for the effect of solid solution strengthening due to Zr additions. Therefore, although the increase in yield strength achieved by increasing the Zr of the as-cast alloys was nonsignificant, the ductility of the alloys remained mostly unchanged. The grain size can be refined effectively after hot rolling, and refined grains contain more grain boundaries that accumulate more strain energy, which reduces the initial recrystallization temperature. Therefore, the sample that underwent HR50CR70 processing had a low initial recrystallization temperature. reading.lever: Apply targeted high-temperature thermomechanical processing (hot rolling followed by controlled annealing) to refine grains and stabilize nano-scale precipitates.
reading.why: This route, successful in Ti-rich MEAs, can improve elevated-temperature strength and microstructural stability in a Ti–Ni primary HEA, addressing current performance limitations.
